documents: g22_W4224281163.pdf: EarthArXiv preprint 'Quantifying Rates of Landscape Unzipping' (Harrison, McElroy, Willenbring), with an author cover letter on p. 1; 39 PDF pages

entry.evidence: We developed a new derivation for valley head retreat rates from the concentration of in situ produced cosmogenic radionuclides in valley walls.

steps.action: Rewrote the Lal (1988) in situ accumulation equation with the chain rule to relate the horizontal concentration gradient to migration rate (Eq. 3; simplified Eq. 4), stating the inheritance and negligible-erosion assumptions.
steps.quote: This can be accomplished by applying the chain rule to the first term in Eq 1.

steps.action: Chose segment A of the seepage-fed Beaverdam Creek network (Apalachicola Bluffs, Florida) as the application site and noted from excavation and topography that springs lack stratigraphic control and valley width is nearly constant.
steps.quote: We applied this theory to a young and rapidly growing channel network, Beaverdam Creek,

steps.action: Designed the sampling: a six-sample upland depth profile plus a 5 m shielded sample for age, uplift and inheritance, and five valley-wall samples along a 460 m axial transect about 5 m below the upland at 0.3 m depth.
steps.quote: To constrain the valley migration rate, we collected five samples along an axial transect at approximately equal elevations.

steps.action: Extracted Be from quartz and measured 10Be/9Be by AMS at PRIME Lab; the depth profile showed a mixed zone to about 1 m and an exponential decrease below.
steps.quote: showed vertical mixing between ~0.5 and 1 m

steps.action: Inverted the depth profile with a Bayesian MCMC (DREAM(zs), Laloy et al. 2017 code; five chains, burn-in 2500) for erosion rate (mode 10 mm/ky), exposure age (median 2.1 My, IQR 1.7-2.5 My) and inheritance.
steps.quote: The erosion rate was well resolved with a clear mode at 10 mm/ky.

steps.action: Measured the transect concentrations (2.9 to 3.5 x 10^5 atoms/g), which decrease toward the steephead.
steps.quote: Concentrations decreased linearly with distance from the downstream end of the valley toward the steephead

steps.action: Fitted a least-squares line to concentration against distance to estimate the spatial gradient (160 atoms/g/m).
steps.quote: It was found to be 160 atoms/g/m with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.90 and a p-value of 0.013.

steps.action: Tested the gradient against the null hypothesis of a spurious trend at the 5% level.
steps.quote: At the 5% confidence level we rejected the null hypothesis that the trend was spurious

steps.action: Combined the gradient with the production and decay terms in Eq. 3 to obtain a valley head retreat rate of 0.025 m/y.
steps.quote: giving a result of V=0.025 m/y

steps.action: Recomputed the rate with the simplified Eq. 4 (no decay term) and obtained the same value.
steps.quote: The decay rate is small, even for the largest measured concentration, and therefore, the simplified equation 4 produces the same result.

steps.action: Compared the length implied by the upland age and the rate (about 50 km) with the actual network length (about 4 km), which gives a mismatch.
steps.quote: implies an overall channel length of ~50 km assuming steady growth

steps.action: Listed four rivals for the mismatch (truncation by the Apalachicola, time-varying rate, flank erosion biasing 10Be, young 160 ky network at constant rate) and favoured climate-driven fluctuation of growth rates.
steps.quote: This implies that either: 1) a significant portion of the channel length has been eroded by the Apalachicola River

steps.action: Compared the rate with the Abrams et al. (2009) groundwater-sapping model (time-averaged 0.0053 m/y) and cited paleoclimate, palynology and speleothem records of Quaternary precipitation variation in support of intermittent growth.
steps.quote: implies a growth rate four-times greater than the time-integrated velocity given by Abrams et al. (2009)

steps.action: Read the near-linear transect trend as steady retreat within segment A, placing any fluctuations before this segment opened.
steps.quote: indicates that the retreat rate has been approximately steady throughout the time that this segment has been incised

steps.action: Kept open the rival that the network is about 160 ky old and grew at a constant rate, possibly initiated by knickpoint migration or drainage reorganization of the Apalachicola.
steps.quote: We also cannot discount the hypothesis that the Beaverdam Creek network is ~160 ky old

steps.action: Derived inheritance-corrected exposure ages for the transect samples with the CRONUS calculator (segment A about 25 ky, against about 20 ky from the gradient) and noted that the southern tributary has migrated further upstream.
steps.quote: we find that segment A began forming ~25 ky ago, in fitting with an overall river network age of 160 ky.

steps.action: Computed the concentration patterns predicted by alternative exposure histories: non-steady unzipping and pauses (Fig. 6), and uniform or tip-increasing valley-flank erosion for channels forming in 20, 100 or 200 ky (Fig. 7).
steps.quote: We numerically modeled the impact of different exposure histories

steps.action: Compared the scenarios: flank erosion gives non-linear profiles only over long formation times; fast formation makes the scenarios indistinguishable.
steps.quote: If the channel forms quickly (e.g., Fig. 7a) the nuclide concentrations are similar regardless of the scenario conditions.

steps.action: Since the flank-erosion rival could not be rejected from the pattern for a 25 ky segment, checked the no-erosion premise by computing the apparent wall erosion rate from the measured concentrations (<10^-5 m/y).
steps.quote: an a posteriori demonstration that the negligible erosion assumption holds.

steps.action: Converted the interquartile surface age and the 67 m elevation of a deltaic to shallow-marine deposit into a relative uplift rate for the Florida panhandle.
steps.quote: this amount of uplift requires overall relative uplift rates between 0.027 and 0.038 mm/y since the Mid-Pleistocene

steps.action: Compared the uplift rate with Opdyke et al. (1984) and with the Adams et al. (2010) karst-isostasy model (about 0.04 mm/y on the Atlantic coast).
steps.quote: The results of the Adams et al. (2010) model predict uplift rates around 0.04 mm/y (40 m/My) along the Atlantic coast.

steps.action: Used the upland surface age as an estimate of when accumulation of the uppermost Citronelle Fm ceased (about 2 My).
steps.quote: the age estimate of ~2 My is an appropriate regional age of formation for the uppermost Citronelle Fm.

steps.action: Derived the method's maximum and minimum resolvable velocities from measurement uncertainty and production-decay equilibrium (Eqs. 7-11): about 1 m/y and 10^-6 m/y, with erosion lowering both bounds.
steps.quote: it is realistic that measurement of topographic features with migration velocities as high as 1 m/y could be achieved.

steps.action: Kept the gradient method as a straightforward estimator of horizontal migration rates, insensitive to spatially constant inheritance, within a stated velocity range.
steps.quote: This method is insensitive to issues associated with inheritance as long as the inherited nuclide concentration is a constant function of space

steps.action: Kept the 0.025 m/y headward growth estimate and left two interpretations of network history (climate-driven intermittent growth, or a young network of about 160 ky) as equally consistent with the data.
steps.quote: An alternative interpretation equally in fitting with the data is that the opening of the seepage valley network began just ~160 ky

tree.answer: Headward migration (unzipping) of seepage valley heads, taken as real from field morphology
No; the rate is latent and inferred from the 10Be gradient through the derived forward relation
Quantify lateral migration rates with a new cosmogenic-gradient method and apply it
Four rivals for the mismatch between age and length; flank erosion as a rival for the gradient
Simulated exposure histories give linear or non-linear profiles, but these are indistinguishable for fast formation
Found: one natural channel segment sampled from traces
Partly: null-trend test, Eq. 4 recomputation, exposure-age cross-check, a posteriori erosion check
Rate kept; network history left between two rivals
Not shown; preprint without a review file

end.claim: Horizontal 10Be concentration gradients give migration rates of topographic features, characterized for a 10^-6 to about 1 m/y range, and applied at Beaverdam Creek they yield a valley head retreat rate of about 0.025 m/y.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the chain-rule rewriting of the accumulation equation into Eqs. 3 and 4, linking migration rate to the along-axis concentration gradient, neither the rate nor the method claim would exist.

gates.evidence: The derived theory (a gradient expected along the valley axis) frames the axial transect design (p. 12, 14), but sampling dates (2010-2011, p. 15) relative to the derivation are not stated. The gradient faced a null-trend test it could have failed (p. 17) and the no-erosion premise an a posteriori check (p. 25). The 0.025 m/y rate has no stated uncertainty and the network interpretation is left between two rivals (p. 30). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: DREAM(zs) differential-evolution MCMC sampler for Bayesian inversion
Pearson correlation and null-hypothesis significance test on the regression slope

novelty_claims.quote: We developed a new derivation for valley head retreat rates from the concentration of in situ produced cosmogenic radionuclides in valley walls.
We present the first empirical data on the growth rate of a well-studied seepage channel network in Florida,
This work supplies the first empirical data on the kinematics of network growth

limits: Coded from the EarthArXiv preprint. The DOI given is the later JGR Earth Surface version, which was not supplied, and no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The 0.025 m/y headward rate is a single estimate from five samples on one transect of one segment, reported without an uncertainty (sub-claim status: estimate_with_resolution, resolution not stated). The uplift rate of 0.027-0.038 mm/y is estimate_with_resolution (interquartile range of the age posterior). The network-history interpretation is best_explanation but explicitly unresolved between two rivals. The stated velocity range is inconsistent across the paper (10^0 m/y in the abstract, 10^1 m/y in the conclusions). The gradient is given as 160 atoms/g/y on p. 18, a unit slip. The text does not say whether the theory preceded the 2010-2011 sampling (inference: the derivation may have followed the data). The prior for erosion is described as Gaussian with an 'upper bound' of 40 mm/ky without explanation. MCMC convergence is reported only through trace plots. The flank-erosion rival is not excluded by the concentration pattern; it is set aside by an a posteriori apparent erosion rate.

disagreements.target: Abrams et al. (2009) groundwater-sapping growth model
disagreements.support: The measured gradient gives a rate about four times the model's time-averaged growth rate, which the authors attribute to non-steady, climate-modulated growth rather than to model error.
disagreements.quote: implies a growth rate four-times greater than the time-integrated velocity given by Abrams et al. (2009)

disagreements.target: Standard practice of subtracting shielded-sample inheritance from surface concentrations
disagreements.support: The derivation shows that a rate follows from the gradient alone when inheritance is spatially constant or small.
disagreements.quote: Our approach does not require a subtraction of the inherited component

disagreements.target: Schmidt (1985) Plio-Pleistocene age assignment of the Citronelle Fm
disagreements.support: The depth-profile exposure age supplies an absolute age of about 2 My for the uppermost Citronelle Fm at Alum Bluff.
disagreements.quote: The Citronelle Fm was previously reported as Plio-Pleistocene in origin with very little absolute age control (Schmidt, 1985).

disagreements.target: Adams et al. (2010) uplift model for north Florida
disagreements.support: The interquartile uplift rates (0.027-0.038 mm/y) sit slightly below the model's 0.04 mm/y, which would need a 1.6 My surface age; the authors still call the two consistent.
disagreements.quote: This result would be consistent with a surface age of 1.6 My in our modeled depth profile.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Gradient-based rate without subtracting inheritance, assuming inheritance is spatially constant or small
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Subtracting the mean shielded-sample concentration; first measuring surface ages
alternatives_considered.reason: Inheritance adds uncertainty to ages; ages are not needed to compute lateral migration rates
Decay is small even for the largest concentration

alternatives_considered.chosen: Climate-driven intermittent growth, with a young (about 160 ky) constant-rate network kept as an equal alternative
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Truncation of the channel by the Apalachicola River; lateral flank erosion lowering 10Be
alternatives_considered.reason: Paleoclimate records of precipitation change; the linear trend in segment A; the a posteriori erosion check
